    ABSTRACT                                                                                                             ARTICLE HISTORY
    Background: Chronic alcohol misuse is associated with alcoholic myopathy, characterized by                           Received 14 July 2021
    skeletal muscle weakness and atrophy. Moreover, there is evidence that sports-related people                         Revised 1 February 2022
    seem to exhibit a greater prevalence of problematic alcohol consumption, especially binge drinking                   Accepted 8 February 2022
    (BD), which might not cause alcoholic myopathy but can negatively impact muscle function and                         KEYWORDS
    amateur and professional athletic performance.                                                                       Alcohol; alcoholic myopathy;
    Objective: To review the literature concerning the effects of alcohol consumption on skeletal muscle                 muscle performance;
    function and structure that can affect muscle performance.                                                           problematic alcohol
    Methodology: We examined the currently available literature (PubMed, Google Scholars) to develop                     consumption; muscle
    a narrative review summarizing the knowledge about the effects of alcohol on skeletal muscle function                pathology; binge drinking
    and exercise performance, obtained from studies in human beings and animal models for problematic
    alcohol consumption.
    Results: Exercise- and sport-based studies indicate that alcohol consumption can negatively affect
    muscle recovery after vigorous exercise, especially in men, while women seem less affected. Clinical
    studies and pre-clinical laboratory research have led to the knowledge of some of the mechanisms
    involved in alcohol-related muscle dysfunction, including an imbalance between anabolic and
    catabolic pathways, reduced regeneration, increased inflammation and fibrosis, and deficiencies
    in energetic balance and mitochondrial function. These pathological features can appear not only
    under chronic alcohol misuse but also in other alcohol consumption patterns.
    Conclusions: Most laboratory-based studies use chronic or acute alcohol exposure, while episodic
    BD, the most common drinking pattern in amateur and professional athletes, is underrepresented.
    Nevertheless, alcohol consumption negatively affects skeletal muscle health through different
    mechanisms, which collectively might contribute to reduced sports performance.
    RESUMEN
    Introduccion: El consumo crónico del alcohol se ha asociado al desarrollo de la miopatía alcohólica,
    una condición del músculo esquelético que se caracteriza por debilitamiento muscular y atrofia. Por
    otro lado, la evidencia sugiere que existe una alta prevalencia del consumo problemático de alcohol
    en deportistas, lo que ocurre principalmente en un patrón por atracón (Binge Drinking, BD, en ingles)
    y que puede impactar negativamente la funcion muscular, y por lo tanto, el desempeño deportivo.
    Objetivo: Revisar en la literatura los efectos del consumo del alcohol en la estructura y función
    del músculo esquelético que podrían afectar el rendimiento deportivo.
    Metodología: Se realizó una revisión de la literatura actualizada, desarrollando un artículo narrativo
    sobre el consumo del alcohol en la función del músculo esquelético y el rendimiento en el ejercicio,
    que recopila conocimientos obtenidos de estudios en humanos y modelos animales de consumo
    problemático del alcohol.
    Resultados: Los estudios basados en deporte y ejercicio sugieren que el consumo de alcohol afecta
    negativamente la recuperación del músculo esquelético luego de un ejercicio vigoroso, especialmente
    en hombres, mientras que las mujeres se parecen menos afectadas. Por otro lado, estudios clínicos y pre-
    clínicos han permitido conocer algunos de los mecanismos involucrados en la disfunción muscular
    ocasionada por el alcohol, los que incluyen un desbalance entre las vías anabólicas y catabólicas,
    regeneración deficiente, un aumento en la inflamación y fibrosis, y desbalances en el equilibrio
    energético y la función mitocondrial. Estos mecanismos patológicos pueden ocurrir no solo en el

    consumo crónico de alcohol, sino que en otros patrones de consumo también.
    Conclusiones: La mayoría de las investigaciones se han concentrado en evaluar los efectos de la
    exposición a alcohol aguda o crónica en el músculo esquelético, mientras que el BD, el patrón de
    consumo más común y frecuente en deportistas aficionados y profesionales ha sido poco estudiado. No
    obstante, el consumo de alcohol afecta negativamente la salud del músculo esquelético a través de
    mecanismos que podrían contribuir a reducir el rendimiento deportivo.

Figure 2. Cellular and molecular alterations in problematic drinking that lead to muscle wasting. Skeletal muscle damage associated
with heavy and chronic alcohol consumption is characterized by an imbalance in mechanisms and signaling pathways that regulates
anabolism/catabolism, decreasing muscle mass: decreased protein translation (2), enhanced protein degradation (5), and increased
autophagy (3). Other molecular features of alcohol-related myopathy are increased inflammation (7), fibrotic response and exacer­
bated extracellular matrix accumulation (1), and mitochondrial dysfunction with increased oxidative stress (4). Also, the reduced
regeneration capacity of the muscle (6) has been described, although most the research in this field come from studies in
immunodeficient animals, and more research is needed to determine if the same alcohol effects are observed in healthy individuals.
In the table, we summarize for each process the main molecular markers that have been found increased (↑) or decreased (↓) in
response to alcohol, indicating in brackets the published references. (*) indicate molecular markers that have been found no changed

{
 "id":"Q81",
 "sourceFile":"The effects of regular cold-water immersion use on training-induced changes in strength and endurance performance - A systematic review with meta-analysis.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title in text 'The Effects of Regular Cold-Water Immersion Use on Training-Induced Changes in Strength and Endurance Performance: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis' matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain":"Recovery & Readiness",
 "domains":["Recovery & Readiness","Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Athletic Training","Coaching"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Adult / Recreational"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Systematic review and meta-analysis of 8 controlled trials (470 volunteers, healthy men classed as trained, physically active, recreationally active or sedentary) in which regular post-training cold-water immersion at 15 C or below was compared with passive or active recovery for 3 weeks or more. In 5 resistance training studies, cold-water immersion was associated with smaller gains in 1RM, maximal isometric strength, strength endurance and ballistic efforts (overall SMD -0.60, 95% CI -0.87 to -0.33). In 4 endurance training studies, it had no effect on maximal aerobic power or time-trial performance (overall SMD -0.07, 95% CI -0.54 to 0.53).",
 "screeningLimitations":"Only 8 studies were pooled, with 4 to 5 per training type, and mean PEDro quality was moderate (5.3), with high risk of bias for randomisation and blinding. The pooled results cannot separate the effects of water temperature, immersion duration and frequency, and most participants were not competitive athletes.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the null endurance result as showing that regular cold-water immersion is harmless or neutral for all endurance training, when it rests on 4 small studies of recreationally active men.",
 "paper":{
  "year":2020,
  "citation":"Malta ES, Dutra YM, Broatch JR, Bishop DJ, Zagatto AM. The Effects of Regular Cold-Water Immersion Use on Training-Induced Changes in Strength and Endurance Performance: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis. Sports Medicine. 2020.",
  "doi":"10.1007/s40279-020-01362-0",
  "abstract":"Meta-analysis of 8 controlled studies of regular post-training cold-water immersion (CWI) during resistance or endurance training. CWI was associated with smaller strength gains, but did not change endurance performance gains.",
  "tldr":"Regular cold-water immersion after resistance training appears to blunt strength gains. After endurance training it did not change aerobic performance gains in these studies.",
  "methods":"PRISMA systematic review of MEDLINE, CENTRAL and SPORTDiscus searched to 25 November 2019, registered on PROSPERO (CRD42018098898). Included controlled trials with CWI at 15 C or below after training of at least 3 weeks, with baseline and post-training strength or aerobic performance measures; quality was rated with the PEDro scale and risk of bias with the Cochrane tool, and effects were pooled as standardised mean differences.",
  "findings":"In resistance training, CWI reduced gains in 1RM, maximal isometric strength, strength endurance and ballistic efforts (overall SMD -0.60, 95% CI -0.87 to -0.33; p < 0.0001). In endurance training, CWI had no effect on maximal aerobic power or time-trial performance (overall SMD -0.07, 95% CI -0.54 to 0.53; p = 0.71).",
  "limitations":"Eight studies with 470 volunteers, mean PEDro quality 5.3 (moderate), no studies blinded, and most with unclear or high risk of bias for randomisation. Water temperature and duration varied widely across studies, and the endurance and resistance subgroups were small (4 to 5 studies each). Participants were trained, physically active, recreationally active or sedentary men rather than competitive athletes.",
  "practicalImplications":"The authors suggest avoiding regular cold-water immersion during training blocks focused on strength, hypertrophy or power, and say it may be most useful around competition when heavy resistance training is not typical. They note the optimal temperature and duration for training adaptation is unknown.",
  "athleteDev":"For strength, hypertrophy or power blocks, avoid scheduling regular post-session cold-water immersion. For endurance blocks, regular immersion did not change aerobic gains in these studies, so the decision should rest on recovery needs rather than expected adaptation.",
  "rtp":"Cannot inform return-to-sport decisions: all participants were healthy and the outcomes were training adaptations, not injury recovery, rehabilitation or readiness after injury."
 }
}

{
 "id":"Q82",
 "sourceFile":"The effects of relaxation techniques following acute, high intensity football training on parasympathetic reactivation.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title in text 'The effects of relaxation techniques following acute, high intensity football training on parasympathetic reactivation' matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Laboratory / Experimental Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Recovery & Readiness",
 "domains":["Recovery & Readiness","Athlete Wellbeing"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Athletic Training"],
 "sports":["American Football"],
 "populations":["Male Athletes","Collegiate"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Non-randomised, repeated-measures experimental study of 38 Division-I male football players in preseason, each tested in three conditions on different Mondays after a high-intensity training session: 15 minutes of guided mindfulness, 15 minutes of seated rest, or usual post-training activity. Post-intervention heart rate was lower after mindfulness (77.0 bpm) and rest (89.9 bpm) than after no intervention (120.1 bpm), with higher SDNN and rMSSD in both relaxation conditions.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The three conditions were given in a fixed order by week (no intervention, then mindfulness, then rest), so condition is confounded with time, and only one squad and one training session per condition were measured. Group sizes were 35, 36 and 33 against a stated total of 38, and no a priori power analysis was done.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read this as proof that relaxation speeds recovery or improves performance, when it measured short-term heart rate and HRV changes in one squad after single sessions and did not measure performance or readiness.",
 "paper":{
  "year":2023,
  "citation":"Renaghan E, et al. The effects of relaxation techniques following acute, high intensity football training on parasympathetic reactivation. Front Sports Act Living. 2023;5:1267631.",
  "doi":"10.3389/fspor.2023.1267631",
  "abstract":"Thirty-eight Division-I male football players were measured under three post-training conditions: 15 minutes of guided mindfulness, 15 minutes of rest, or no intervention. Both relaxation conditions produced larger drops in heart rate and respiration rate and larger HRV increases than no intervention.",
  "tldr":"A 15-minute guided mindfulness session or a seated rest period after high-intensity football training lowered heart rate and breathing rate and raised HRV more than usual post-training activity. Staff could use either as a low-equipment step, but the effect was measured in one squad over single sessions.",
  "methods":"Repeated-measures, non-randomised design with each athlete tested in all three conditions, one Monday per condition, after routine preseason training. Heart rate, respiration rate, SDNN and rMSSD were recorded with an armband monitor (Warfighter Monitor) before, during and after the 15-minute intervention and analysed by repeated-measures ANOVA with Tukey correction.",
  "findings":"Heart rate fell by 81.6 bpm after mindfulness, 66.4 bpm after rest and 40.9 bpm after no intervention, and both relaxation conditions produced larger falls than no intervention (p < 0.0000). Post-intervention SDNN was 46.9 ms after mindfulness, 42.9 ms after rest and 33.1 ms after no intervention, and rMSSD was 17.9, 16.7 and 13.8 ms respectively.",
  "limitations":"Condition order was fixed by week, so condition and time cannot be separated, and the design is not randomised. Group sizes (35, 36, 33) do not match the stated sample of 38, no a priori power analysis was run, and four authors are employees of Tiger Tech Solutions, which makes the Warfighter Monitor.",
  "practicalImplications":"A 15-minute guided mindfulness session or seated rest straight after a high-intensity session is a low-equipment way to lower heart rate and raise HRV. In this study mindfulness produced larger falls in heart rate and breathing rate and larger HRV increases than rest, so it is the stronger option.",
  "athleteDev":"Use a 15-minute block of guided breathing or seated rest in the minutes after hard training to bring heart rate down, and track HRV to see the response. The study did not measure performance, so it does not show that this improves performance.",
  "rtp":"Cannot inform return-to-sport decisions: it tested uninjured starters after single training sessions, with no injured or returning players and no readiness or performance outcomes."
 }
}

{
 "id":"Q83",
 "sourceFile":"The effects of repeated sprint training on physical fitness and physiological adaptation in athletes - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title in text 'The Effects of Repeated-Sprint Training on Physical Fitness and Physiological Adaptation in Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis' matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain":"Training & Performance",
 "domains":["Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Coaching","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport","Soccer","Basketball","Volleyball","Rugby","Other Sport"],
 "populations":["Healthy Athletes","Youth / Adolescent","Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis of 40 publications (48 repeated-sprint training groups with 541 athletes, and 19 active control groups with 213 athletes), with running repeated-sprint training of 2 to 12 weeks in healthy, trained athletes aged 14 to 35. Pooled effects (Hedges g, Table 2) were improvements in VO2max (0.63, 90% CI 0.36 to 0.91) and YYIR1 distance (0.60), a reduced RSA decrement (-0.63), and smaller gains in 10 m and 20 m sprint (-0.34 and -0.45), RSA average time (-0.34), CMJ height (0.27) and change-of-direction ability (-0.32). Changing frequency, duration, weekly volume, reps, sets or distance from the reference program gave no clear benefit.",
 "screeningLimitations":"Most studies ran repeated-sprint training alongside usual training with no isolated comparison, so the true effect of the training alone is unknown. Several programming moderators were tested only by univariate analysis or qualitative synthesis, so their evidence is weaker.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could treat the reference program (3 sets of 6 x 30 m, twice weekly for 6 weeks) as a proven optimal dose, when it is only the comparison point the moderator analyses used.",
 "paper":{
  "year":2023,
  "citation":"Thurlow F, et al. The Effects of Repeated-Sprint Training on Physical Fitness and Physiological Adaptation in Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Sports Medicine. 2023.",
  "doi":"10.1007/s40279-023-01959-1",
  "abstract":"Systematic review and meta-analysis of 40 studies of running-based repeated-sprint training (RST) in trained athletes aged 14 to 35. RST produced moderate gains in VO2max, Yo-Yo intermittent recovery distance and repeated-sprint decrement, and small gains in sprint, repeated-sprint average time, jump and change-of-direction measures. Changes to programming compared with a reference program gave little clear benefit.",
  "tldr":"Running repeated-sprint training improves aerobic fitness, intermittent running, sprint speed and jump height in trained athletes. Three sets of six 30 m sprints, twice weekly for 6 weeks, is a well-supported starting prescription.",
  "methods":"PRISMA systematic review of PubMed, SPORTDiscus and Scopus searched to 4 July 2023, registered on the Open Science Framework. Included trained or higher-calibre athletes aged 14 to 35 in running RST of 10 s or less with 60 s or less rest for 2 to 12 weeks; quality was rated with a modified Downs and Black index, and multilevel meta-analysis and meta-regression were run against a reference program of three sets of 6 x 30 m, twice weekly for 6 weeks.",
  "findings":"Pooled effects (Table 2, 90% CI) were VO2max 0.63 (0.36 to 0.91), YYIR1 0.60 (0.43 to 0.77), RSA decrement -0.63 (-0.86 to -0.40), 10 m sprint -0.34 (-0.47 to -0.21), 20 m sprint -0.45 (-0.69 to -0.21), CMJ height 0.27 (0.14 to 0.39) and change of direction -0.32 (-0.53 to -0.12). Compared with the reference program, one more session per week, one more week, 200 m more volume, two more reps, one more set or 10 m more distance was either non-substantial or came with compatibility with impairment in at least one outcome.",
  "limitations":"The abstract's effect sizes differ from Table 2 (VO2max 0.56 vs 0.63, 20 m sprint -0.48 vs -0.45, RSA decrement -0.61 vs -0.63, YYIR1 0.61 vs 0.60, CMJ 0.26 vs 0.27). Table 3 lists VO2max as 2.6 ml/kg/min while the text gives 2.2, and the YYIR1 raw-unit CI reads '1534 to 296', which is a typo. Most studies were non-randomised or non-controlled, and the review could not separate sprint modality or rest duration in its models.",
  "practicalImplications":"Three sets of six 30 m straight-line sprints with 20 s passive rest, twice weekly for 6 weeks, is an effective default block. Four sets per session added to intermittent running gains, and a third weekly session impaired change-of-direction ability, so the authors advise against three weekly sessions outside short 2-week blocks.",
  "athleteDev":"Use 3 sets of 6 x 30 m, twice weekly for 6 weeks, as a time-efficient block, with 4 to 6 reps per set. A third weekly session did not add benefit and impaired change of direction in the reference comparison, so reserve it for short shock blocks.",
  "rtp":"Limited return-to-sport use: the authors mention late-stage return-to-play as a possible use, but all included athletes were healthy and uninjured, so the data cannot set return-to-play sprint loads."
 }
}

{
 "id":"Q84",
 "sourceFile":"The effects of travel on performance a - 13 year analysis of the National Rugby League NRL competition.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title in text 'The effects of travel on performance: a 13-year analysis of the National Rugby League (NRL) competition' matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Other",
 "primaryDomain":"Recovery & Readiness",
 "domains":["Recovery & Readiness","Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["Rugby"],
 "populations":["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Retrospective analysis of official NRL match results from 2007 to 2019 (2,352 league matches, 4,704 team observations), coded as Other because it is a match-record analysis rather than a cohort or survey. For every 1,000 km of away travel, estimated win probability fell by 2.7% (95% CI -5.7 to 0.3%) and points difference by 1.1 points (95% CI -2.0 to -0.2), with the travel effect smaller in later seasons and no clear differences between states.",
 "screeningLimitations":"Travel was measured as straight-line distance between home venues, so actual route, time zones, and travel outside matches are not captured. The win-probability interval includes zero, so only the points-difference effect is clearly different from zero.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could treat the 2.7% win-probability loss as a reliable per-trip effect for their own team, when the interval crosses zero and the figures are league-wide averages.",
 "paper":{
  "year":2022,
  "citation":"Read DB, Williams S, Fullagar HHK, Weakley JJS. The effects of travel on performance: a 13-year analysis of the National Rugby League (NRL) competition. Science and Medicine in Football. 2022;6(1):60-65.",
  "doi":"10.1080/24733938.2021.1876243",
  "abstract":"Analysis of 2,352 NRL matches (2007 to 2019) found that longer away travel was associated with a lower chance of winning and a smaller points difference. The effect of travel shrank over the 13 seasons, with no clear differences between states.",
  "tldr":"In the NRL, each 1,000 km of away travel was linked to a small drop in winning chances and in points margin. The effect has shrunk over time, but the win-probability estimate is imprecise.",
  "methods":"Exploratory retrospective analysis of official NRL match results from 2007 to 2019, excluding draws, play-offs and matches played away from the home city. Win or loss was modelled with a generalised linear mixed model and points difference with a linear mixed model, with team nested within season as a random effect; travel was the straight-line distance from each team's home venue.",
  "findings":"Each 1,000 km of travel reduced win probability by 2.7% (95% CI -5.7 to 0.3%) and points difference by 1.1 points (95% CI -2.0 to -0.2). The away team had an odds ratio of 0.56 (0.48 to 0.66) for winning, and the travel effect was largest in 2007 to 2009 (-2.7%, 95% CI -4.7 to -0.6%) and close to zero in 2018 to 2019.",
  "limitations":"Travel outside matches, sleep, and individual player data were not available, and the effect of team quality was only partly controlled. The authors note that a team-by-team analysis is needed, and the single Victorian team showed no travel penalty, so the league average may not describe individual teams.",
  "practicalImplications":"Coaches can estimate the likely effect of an away trip on match outcome and use it when planning travel logistics, sleeping arrangements and nutrition. The authors note that teams travelling more than 2,000 km for away matches could expect about 2.2 fewer points and a 5.4% lower winning likelihood on average.",
  "athleteDev":"Use the travel distance of an away fixture as a planning input for sleep, meals and logistics, because longer trips were linked to small average performance losses in this league. The study does not show that any specific travel strategy reduces those losses.",
  "rtp":"Does not inform return to sport: it analyses team match results for players in the competition, with no injury, rehabilitation or return-to-play data."
 }
}

 "evidenceSummary":"Systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 randomised trials (308 participants, mostly men, aged about 14 to 24, with prior resistance training experience) comparing back-squat training with low (0 to 20%) and high (30 to 45%) velocity loss thresholds for 6 to 8 weeks. Within groups, both ranges improved 1RM, heavy-load and light-load squat velocity and CMJ height, while only low thresholds improved 20 m sprint time; between groups, heavy-load, light-load and sprint gains were larger with low thresholds (p < 0.05), and the CMJ difference was not significant (p = 0.088).",
 "screeningLimitations":"Only 13 studies were included, all 6 to 8 weeks long, squat-only, and with few CMJ or sprint training components. Allocation concealment was unclear in all studies, and the meta-regression used only linear-progression studies.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the per-goal velocity loss ranges (Table 3) as settled prescriptions, when the interaction p values were 0.076 for CMJ and 0.010 for sprint and the CMJ between-group result was not significant.",
 "paper":{
  "year":2024,
  "citation":"Chen BY, et al. The effects of velocity loss thresholds during resistance training on lower-limb performance enhancement: A systematic review with meta-analysis. International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching. 2024:1-15.",
  "doi":"10.1177/17479541241244581",
  "abstract":"Meta-analysis of 13 studies (308 participants) of back-squat training with low (0 to 20%) or high (30 to 45%) velocity loss thresholds. Low thresholds gave larger heavy-load squat velocity, light-load squat velocity and sprint gains, while maximal strength gains were similar between thresholds.",
  "tldr":"Squat sets stopped at about 20% velocity loss gave better speed and power gains than sets allowed to lose 30 to 45%, while maximal strength changed similarly. Coaches may prefer low thresholds when speed or power is the goal.",
  "methods":"PRISMA systematic review (PROSPERO CRD42021247929) of five databases searched in May 2023. Included peer-reviewed randomised trials of back-squat training of at least 4 weeks that used velocity monitoring and ended sets at a set velocity loss threshold; effects were pooled as Hedges g with random-effects models, and meta-regression was run on linear-progression studies only.",
  "findings":"Between-group differences favoured low thresholds for heavy-load squat velocity (ES -0.40, p = 0.005), light-load squat velocity (ES -0.39, p = 0.025) and sprint time (ES -0.47, p = 0.022). The CMJ difference (ES -0.24, p = 0.088) and 1RM difference (ES -0.65, p = 0.630) were not significant.",
  "limitations":"The abstract and discussion describe the CMJ advantage of low thresholds as superior although p = 0.088, which is not significant. The sprint meta-regression p value is 0.010 in the abstract and discussion but 0.002 in the results. High-threshold group labels also vary between 30 to 40% and 30 to 45% across the text and figures, and the studies were short, squat-only programs.",
  "practicalImplications":"For speed or jump goals, stopping sets at about 10 to 20% velocity loss is the best-supported range, with sprint gains most consistent at 10% or less. For maximal strength alone, a 0 to 40% range gave similar gains in the authors' table, so tight control may not be needed.",
  "athleteDev":"Use a velocity loss of 20% or less on squat sets when the goal is speed, power or jump height, and 10% or less when sprint time is the priority. Strength-only blocks can tolerate wider thresholds, but the review did not test these over a full training season.",
  "rtp":"Cannot inform return to sport: all included trials used healthy, non-injured, resistance-trained people, and no rehabilitation or return-to-play outcomes were assessed."
 }
}

{
 "id":"Q86",
 "sourceFile":"The evidence for common nonsurgical modalities in sports medicine, Part 1 - Kinesio tape, sports massage therapy, and acupuncture.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title in text 'The Evidence for Common Nonsurgical Modalities in Sports Medicine, Part 1: Kinesio Tape, Sports Massage Therapy, and Acupuncture' matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain":"Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains":["Sports Medicine & Injury","Rehabilitation & Return to Sport","Recovery & Readiness"],
 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Athletic Training","Rehabilitation"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Review article of publications from 2006 to 2019 found through PubMed and Google Scholar on Kinesio taping, sports massage therapy and acupuncture. The authors report low-level evidence for a small, short-term pain and range-of-motion effect of Kinesio tape (suggested for athletes with acute shoulder symptoms before activity), acupuncture for carpal tunnel syndrome and as an adjunct for low back pain, and little or conflicting evidence for sports massage or acupuncture effects on performance.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The method is described only as PubMed and Google Scholar searches with no search terms, eligibility criteria or appraisal method, so it is a narrative review rather than a systematic one. Most cited trials are small, with short follow-up and limited blinding.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the performance section as evidence that taping, massage or acupuncture improves athletic performance, when the authors found little, small or conflicting evidence for performance outcomes.",
 "paper":{
  "year":2020,
  "citation":"Trofa DP, et al. The Evidence for Common Nonsurgical Modalities in Sports Medicine, Part 1: Kinesio Tape, Sports Massage Therapy, and Acupuncture. JAAOS Glob Res Rev. 2020;4(1):e19.00104.",
  "doi":"10.5435/JAAOSGlobal-D-19-00104",
  "abstract":"Narrative review of Kinesio taping, sports massage therapy and acupuncture in athletes and patients with musculoskeletal conditions, drawn from publications from 2006 to 2019. The evidence is low-level, with small, short-term effects for some uses and little evidence for sports performance.",
  "tldr":"Kinesio tape may be reasonable for athletes with shoulder symptoms before activity, but the benefit is small and short-term. Acupuncture has some support for carpal tunnel syndrome and as a low back pain adjunct, and evidence for sports massage and performance is weak.",
  "methods":"Narrative review of publications from 2006 to 2019 found through PubMed and Google Scholar, covering three modalities: Kinesio taping, sports massage therapy and acupuncture. No search terms, eligibility criteria or risk-of-bias method are reported.",
  "findings":"Kinesio tape trials showed short-term pain or range-of-motion changes, with no sustained benefit and conflicting strength results. Sports massage gave short-term shoulder and neck pain relief, and performance results were mixed (one study found higher jump height and less soreness, another no change in sprint speed). Acupuncture gave short-term carpal tunnel and low back pain benefit, while its performance evidence was conflicting.",
  "limitations":"The method is described only as a PubMed and Google Scholar search, so coverage is unknown and selection cannot be checked. The authors describe most trials as small, unblinded and short-term, and several authors disclose financial relationships with Arthrex, Smith and Nephew, and Stryker.",
  "practicalImplications":"The review supports trying Kinesio tape before activity for athletes with acute shoulder symptoms, with the expectation of a small, short-lived effect. Acupuncture can be considered as an adjunct for low back pain or carpal tunnel symptoms, and sports massage for short-term symptom relief.",
  "athleteDev":"Kinesio tape is a low-cost option for athletes with shoulder symptoms before activity, but do not expect it to change strength or sprint performance. The review found no firm support for massage or acupuncture as performance aids.",
  "rtp":"Partly relevant: the review covers shoulder symptoms and low back pain, but it gives no return-to-play criteria or return-to-sport outcomes, so it cannot set return-to-sport timing."
 }
}

  "rtp":"Partly relevant: alcohol after eccentric exercise damage slowed strength recovery in the cited work, but the review includes no injured athletes or return-to-sport tests and cannot set return-to-play timing."
